source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure all images have a text alternative so any user can understand image content.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: text alternatives (Perceivable principle). Any information conveyed in an image must also be available as text, so users who cannot see the image are not excluded.
example_good: All images include descriptive alt text conveying the same information as the image.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Provide equivalent text alternatives for all video and audio content.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: time-based media (Perceivable principle). Users who cannot access audio or video must be able to access equivalent information through transcripts or captions.
example_good: Video includes captions and audio includes a transcript.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Do not rely on colour or sound alone to convey meaning.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: distinguishable (Perceivable principle). Users who cannot perceive colour differences or audio cues must be able to access the same information through another means such as text labels or patterns.
example_bad: A red border used alone to indicate an error field.
example_good: A red border plus a visible text label 'Error' to indicate an error field.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure content can be presented in different ways without losing information or structure.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: adaptable (Perceivable principle). Content must not depend on a specific visual layout or presentation. Users who change display settings such as font size or orientation must still be able to access all information.
example_good: Content remains meaningful when styles are removed or screen orientation is changed.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure all content is operable by keyboard alone.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: keyboard accessible (Operable principle). Users who cannot use a mouse must be able to access and operate all content and interface elements using only a keyboard.
example_good: All interactive elements are reachable and usable via keyboard Tab and Enter keys.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure timed content gives users enough time to read and interact.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: enough time (Operable principle). Users who read or process information slowly must be able to control or extend any time limits on content.
example_bad: Auto-advancing carousel with no pause control.
example_good: Carousel includes pause/stop controls so users can read at their own pace.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Do not create content that causes seizures or physical reactions.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: seizures and physical reactions (Operable principle). Content must not include flashing elements that exceed safe thresholds, as this can trigger seizures in susceptible users.
example_bad: Rapidly flashing animation exceeding 3 flashes per second.
example_good: Static or slow-transition animation within safe flash thresholds.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure users can navigate content and know where they are on the page.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: navigable (Operable principle). Content must include navigation aids such as page titles, headings, and skip links so users can find information and orient themselves.
example_good: Page includes a descriptive title and logical heading structure to aid navigation.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure content is operable with input methods other than a keyboard such as a pointer.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: input modalities (Operable principle). Users who interact via touch, stylus, or other pointer devices must be able to operate all content.
example_good: All interactive elements have sufficient touch target size and are usable by pointer input.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Write text that can be read and understood including unusual words and shortened forms.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: readable (Understandable principle). Text must be comprehensible to users, with unusual words explained and language of the page declared so assistive technology can interpret it correctly.
example_good: Abbreviations are expanded on first use and the page language is set in the HTML lang attribute.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Design content so users can predict its appearance and how to operate it.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: predictable (Understandable principle). Consistent navigation and behaviour reduce cognitive load and help users anticipate how content works.
example_bad: Navigation changes position or labelling between pages.
example_good: Navigation appears in the same location with the same labels across all pages.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Help users avoid and correct input mistakes.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: input assistance (Understandable principle). Forms and interactive elements must include clear labels and error messages so users can identify and fix mistakes.
example_good: Form fields include descriptive labels and inline error messages that specify what needs to be corrected.

source_heading: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs
rule_summary: Ensure markup supports assistive technology and software used to access content.
rule_detail: WCAG Guideline: compatible (Robust principle). Content must be built with valid markup so screen readers and other assistive technologies can reliably parse and interpret it.
example_good: HTML is valid and uses semantic elements so assistive technology can correctly interpret content structure.

source_heading: Follow Style Manual guidance on accessibility requirements
rule_summary: Check accessibility requirements in the Style Manual callout boxes when writing on any topic.
rule_detail: The Style Manual embeds accessibility requirements as callout boxes throughout topic pages. Writers should look for and apply these requirements as they consult guidance on specific topics, not treat accessibility as a separate concern.
example_good: Accessibility callout boxes are reviewed and applied as part of drafting each content type.

source_heading: People skim headings and page structure
rule_summary: Write clear page titles that align with the first heading on the page.
rule_detail: Screen reader users hear the page title first. It should match or closely align with the first H1 heading to orient all users immediately.
example_good: warn

source_heading: People skim headings and page structure
rule_summary: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rule_detail: Section headings help users navigate and understand where they are on a page. Each heading should describe the topic or the content of the following section.
example_good: warn

source_heading: People skim headings and page structure
rule_summary: Do not rely on colour alone to structure pages.
rule_detail: Colour-only structure is inaccessible to users who cannot distinguish colours. Always pair colour with another structural cue such as shape or text.
example_good: error

source_heading: People skim headings and page structure
rule_summary: Do not rely on sensory characteristics such as shape or visual location to explain things.
rule_detail: Instructions that depend on visual placement (e.g. 'click the button on the right') exclude users who cannot perceive layout. Use explicit labels or text instead.
example_bad: See the button on the left

source_heading: People skim headings and page structure
rule_summary: Present information in accepted patterns such as address blocks and underlined hyperlinks.
rule_detail: Users scan for familiar patterns to find specific information quickly. Deviating from conventions such as underlined links reduces scannability and user trust.
example_good: warn

source_heading: Content with too many unfamiliar words slows readers down
rule_summary: Write in plain language using familiar words.
rule_detail: Familiar words that are spelled as they sound are easier to read. Unfamiliar or complex words cause readers to slow down and may impede comprehension.
example_good: warn
implementation_type: Match tokens against a high-frequency word list and flag low-frequency tokens

source_heading: Content with too many unfamiliar words slows readers down
rule_summary: Avoid double negatives.
rule_detail: Double negatives require extra cognitive effort to decode and can obscure meaning for all readers.
example_good: is important

source_heading: Content with too many unfamiliar words slows readers down
rule_summary: Expand all acronyms on their first use.
rule_detail: Unexplained acronyms are unfamiliar to many readers and slow comprehension. Always spell out the full form at first mention followed by the acronym in parentheses.
example_bad: The DSS will manage the APS reform.
example_good: The Department of Social Services (DSS) will manage the Australian Public Service (APS) reform.

source_heading: Content with too many unfamiliar words slows readers down
rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words phrases idioms and jargon.
rule_detail: Unusual or idiomatic language creates barriers for readers with lower literacy or non-English backgrounds. Where specialist terms are needed provide a plain-language explanation.
example_good: warn
implementation_type: Match tokens against a curated jargon/idiom list and flag unglossed matches

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Aim for an average sentence length of 15 words per sentence.
rule_detail: Short sentences limit the scope of an idea and are easier to process. Most readers benefit from variety but the average should stay around 15 words.
example_good: warn
implementation_type: Compute mean word count per sentence across document; flag if mean exceeds 15

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Keep long sentences to no more than 25 words.
rule_detail: Sentences exceeding 25 words are difficult for many readers to parse in a single pass. Break them into shorter units to maintain clarity.
example_good: error
implementation_type: Count tokens per sentence (excluding punctuation); flag any sentence with more than 25 tokens

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Do not use blocks of capital letters in body text.
rule_detail: All-caps text is harder to read than mixed case. Use capital letters only where grammatically required or for established proper nouns.
example_bad: BLOCKS OF CAPITAL LETTERS ARE HARD TO READ.
example_good: Blocks of capital letters are hard to read.

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Use capital letters appropriately to support comprehension of written English.
rule_detail: Overuse or misuse of capitals disrupts reading rhythm. Apply capitals only according to standard grammar and style rules.
example_good: warn
implementation_type: Flag tokens in non-initial sentence positions that are fully uppercased and are not known proper nouns or acronyms

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Use new paragraphs and line breaks to help readers build reading rhythm.
rule_detail: Paragraphs give readers a rest and help them locate ideas quickly. Well-placed line breaks keep readers focused and prevent ideas from running together.
example_good: info

source_heading: Rhythm changes can help or hinder reading
rule_summary: Avoid line breaks that split ideas at the wrong place or create too many short lines.
rule_detail: Poorly placed line breaks disrupt reading rhythm. Breaks should coincide with natural idea boundaries not mid-thought.
example_good: warn

source_heading: Clear content helps all users
rule_summary: Write content at reading level 2 (Australian year 7 equivalent).
rule_detail: Content should target a year 7 reading level so it is accessible to the majority of Australian adults. About 44% of adults read at literacy level 1 to 2, making plain language essential for broad access.
example_good: Check that your content is a reading level 2 (Australian year 7 equivalent).

source_heading: Accessibility requirements
rule_summary: Write in plain language to meet accessibility requirements.
rule_detail: Plain language is a fundamental accessibility requirement. It helps all users and is essential for those with low literacy. WCAG 3.1.5 requires content to be readable at lower secondary education level (year 7).
example_good: Write in plain language.

source_heading: Accessibility requirements
rule_summary: Avoid unusual words and phrases or explain them when they must be used.
rule_detail: Unusual words, phrases and idioms create barriers for users with low literacy. If an unusual term is unavoidable, provide an explanation. This supports WCAG 3.1.3 (Unusual words).
example_bad: Using jargon or idioms without explanation
example_good: Avoid (or explain) unusual words phrases idioms and so on.
pattern_hint: Flag tokens not in a high-frequency word list (e.g. top 5000 AE words)

source_heading: Accessibility requirements
rule_summary: Expand all acronyms on their first use.
rule_detail: All acronyms and initialisms must be written out in full the first time they appear in a document or page, supporting WCAG 3.1.4 (Abbreviations). This aids users unfamiliar with specialist terminology.
example_good: The Australian Public Service (APS) manages human resources (HR) policy.
pattern_hint: Regex for pattern [A-Z]{2,} not preceded by its expansion earlier in the document

source_heading: Accessibility requirements
rule_summary: Do not use double negatives.
rule_detail: Double negatives make content harder to understand for all readers, especially those with low literacy. Rewrite to express the positive meaning directly.
example_bad: It is not uncommon for applicants to be unsuccessful.
example_good: It is common for applicants to be unsuccessful.
pattern_hint: Detect negation token (not/no) modifying another negated word (e.g. 'not un-', 'not without', 'cannot fail to')

source_heading: Understanding users
rule_summary: Do user research before writing; do not assume all users can read and understand your content.
rule_detail: Writers should not assume a uniform literacy level among their audience. Conduct user research to understand the range of literacy needs and ensure content meets those needs.
example_good: Before you start writing do user research.

source_heading: Understanding users
rule_summary: Ensure users with low literacy have equal access to government services and information.
rule_detail: Content must be accessible regardless of a user's literacy level. Consider alternative channels and formats so that users who cannot engage with written digital content can still access services without repetition or confusion.
example_good: Ensure users with low literacy have equal access.

source_heading: Make content accessible
rule_summary: Design government content to be accessible and inclusive for all users.
rule_detail: Government services and products must be available to everyone. Inclusive content recognises Australia's diversity and the range of technologies and abilities users bring. This is a requirement under the Digital Service Standard.
example_good: Design accessible and inclusive content.

source_heading: Make content accessible
rule_summary: Ensure digital government services are usable and accessible as required by the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: The Digital Service Standard mandates that Australian Government digital services be both usable and accessible. Content creators must follow accessibility guidance to meet this legal and policy obligation.
example_good: Ensure digital services are usable and accessible.

source_heading: Make content accessible
rule_summary: Account for cultural and linguistic diversity when creating content.
rule_detail: Inclusive content must accommodate users from diverse cultural and linguistic backgrounds. Writers should consider whether language choices, examples and references are accessible to users for whom English is not a first language.

source_heading: Make content accessible
rule_summary: Account for diversity of abilities among users when creating content.
rule_detail: Inclusive content must accommodate users with a range of abilities. Content design should not assume all users interact with technology in the same way or have the same physical or cognitive capabilities.

source_heading: Follow accessibility guidance in context
rule_summary: Follow the accessibility requirements provided in each Style Manual topic.
rule_detail: Each Style Manual topic includes specific accessibility callouts indicating what is required. Writers must act on these contextual requirements rather than treating accessibility as a separate concern.

source_heading: Spelling and capitalisation
rule_summary: Do not use diacritical marks in Australian place names.
rule_detail: Australian place names use a standard 26-character alphabet without accent marks or diacritics. When names from other languages are adopted as official Australian place names they lose any diacritical marks.
example_good: D'Entrecasteaux
pattern_hint: Match known place names with diacritics against official spellings

source_heading: Spelling and capitalisation
rule_summary: Do not write Australian place names in possessive form.
rule_detail: Official Australian place names are not possessive. Remove any possessive apostrophe-s from place name usage.
example_good: Baden-Powell Waterhole

source_heading: Spelling and capitalisation
rule_summary: Do not add punctuation to Australian place names unless part of the official name.
rule_detail: Australian place names generally do not have punctuation. Only hyphens and apostrophes that were part of the name of a commemorated person appear in official names.
example_good: Baden-Powell Waterhole

source_heading: Spelling and capitalisation
rule_summary: Capitalise all words in an Australian place name that form part of the proper noun.
rule_detail: Australian place names are proper nouns and require capitalisation. Words that do not usually take a capital letter do so when part of a place name.
example_good: Baden-Powell Waterhole
pattern_hint: Check that all tokens forming a recognised place name are title-cased

source_heading: Punctuation
rule_summary: Separate the two parts of an official dual place name with a spaced forward slash.
rule_detail: When writing official dual names (combining a First Nations name and an English name) use a spaced forward slash between the two parts in the order given in the official record.
example_good: Kata Tjuta / Mount Olga

source_heading: Use capitals for names of places roads and streets
rule_summary: Use an initial capital for every word in the name of a road street or thoroughfare.
rule_detail: The names of roads streets and other thoroughfares take an initial capital even for words that would not normally be capitalised. This applies to streets avenues highways terraces and similar.
example_good: Monaro Highway
pattern_hint: Named entity recognition for streets/roads followed by type word (Street Avenue Road etc) — check title case

source_heading: Use shortened forms for addresses
rule_summary: Do not add punctuation marks to address abbreviations or contractions.
rule_detail: Address shortened forms such as Blvd Av and Rd do not take full stops or other punctuation. Minimal punctuation style applies to all address abbreviations.
example_good: Bendemeer Blvd

source_heading: Shortened state and territory names for addresses
rule_summary: Write the last line of a domestic postal address in full capitals without punctuation or underlining.
rule_detail: The final line of a letter address must contain the place name or post office of delivery in capitals followed by the state or territory abbreviation and postcode with no punctuation.
example_good: 11 Banks Av / WAGGA WAGGA NSW 2650
pattern_hint: Check last line of address block for all-caps town name followed by state abbreviation and postcode

source_heading: Shortened state and territory names for addresses
rule_summary: Spell out all names in full when writing overseas addresses.
rule_detail: When sending mail overseas abbreviate nothing to prevent confusion. For example 'SA' could mean South Australia or South Africa to an international reader.
example_bad: 11 Banks Av, Wagga Wagga SA 2650 [on overseas mail]
example_good: 11 Banks Av, Wagga Wagga South Australia 2650 [on overseas mail]

source_heading: Write the names of buildings structures and public places with an initial capital
rule_summary: Capitalise the names of buildings structures and public places.
rule_detail: Names of buildings structures and public places take initial capitals. When referring to the same place generically afterwards use lower case for the generic term.
example_bad: the cathedral [after naming St Paul's Cathedral]
example_good: St Paul's Cathedral
pattern_hint: NER for building/structure/place names — check initial caps on all name tokens then lower case on subsequent generic reference

source_heading: Write the names of buildings structures and public places with an initial capital
rule_summary: Write generic and plural terms for buildings or structures in lower case.
rule_detail: When a generic term such as 'cathedral' or 'bridge' is used after a proper name or in a plural context it is lowercase. Only the specific proper name takes capitals.
example_bad: The Iron Cove and Gladesville Bridges are both in Sydney.
example_good: The Iron Cove and Gladesville bridges are both in Sydney.
pattern_hint: Detect capitalised generic building/structure type word (Bridge Cathedral Station etc) appearing after a proper noun or in plural context

source_heading: Write the names of buildings structures and public places with an initial capital
rule_summary: Use initial capitals for the names of private properties.
rule_detail: Names of private properties such as stations homesteads and rural holdings take initial capitals just as other proper place names do.
example_good: Thargomindah Station

source_heading: Shorten names for states and territories in 4 situations
rule_summary: Spell out the full names of Australian states and territories in formal content.
rule_detail: Shortened forms of state and territory names are only acceptable in four specific situations: as an adjective when space is limited when repetition would result or in addresses. In formal contexts always write the full name.
example_good: New South Wales Government [in formal document body]
pattern_hint: Detect NSW VIC QLD WA SA TAS ACT NT not used as adjective or in address context in formal text

source_heading: Shorten names for states and territories in 4 situations
rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after shortened forms of state and territory names.
rule_detail: This rule applies to all shortened forms: initialisms (NSW WA ACT NT) abbreviations (Vic Tas) and the contraction (Qld). No full stop is used after any of these forms.
example_good: NSW or Vic

source_heading: Adverbial clauses
rule_summary: Use a comma after an introductory adverbial clause to mark the start of the main clause.
rule_detail: When an adverbial clause precedes the main clause, a comma separates them. Without the comma, the subject of the main clause can be hard to identify.
example_bad: When I met with Eun-jung Deng met with Evelyn.
example_good: When I met with Eun-jung Deng met with Evelyn. → When I met with Eun-jung[
tags: Detect adverbial subordinating conjunction opening a sentence followed by a clause boundary without a comma

source_heading: Conjunctions 'if' and 'whether'
rule_summary: Use 'whether' instead of 'if' when expressing two concrete possibilities.
rule_detail: 'If' is conditional and states a condition for the main clause to be true. 'Whether' indicates two possibilities. Using 'if' where 'whether' is intended can produce ambiguous sentences.
example_bad: We asked if he was working from home or from the office.
example_good: We asked whether he was working from home or from the office.
pattern_hint: Detect 'if' followed by a clause containing 'or', suggesting two possibilities rather than a condition

source_heading: Conjunctions 'if' and 'whether'
rule_summary: Use 'if' only to express a condition and not to introduce two alternatives.
rule_detail: 'If' defines a condition that must exist for the main clause to be true. When two explicit alternatives are present, 'whether' is the correct conjunction.
example_good: We can eat lunch outside if the rain stops.
pattern_hint: Detect 'if' clause without 'or' alternative to confirm conditional use is appropriate

source_heading: Structure items in a series as a list
rule_summary: Do not create a list with only one item.
rule_detail: Lists are for a series of items only. A single item should be incorporated into prose instead. Using a list for one item misrepresents the content structure.

source_heading: Structure items in a series as a list
rule_summary: Always introduce a list with a lead-in phrase or heading.
rule_detail: All lists require a lead-in (a phrase or sentence) or a heading to introduce them. A list without a lead-in lacks context for the reader.

source_heading: Make short lists
rule_summary: Move long lists to a separate page or an appendix.
rule_detail: Long lists lose meaning and hierarchy because lower items are further from the lead-in. If a list is too long, move it out of the main content flow.

source_heading: Limit the number of lists
rule_summary: Avoid using too many lists in a single document or page.
rule_detail: Content with too many lists is hard to follow. Lists should be used selectively so that prose can flow and readers can engage with the content naturally.

source_heading: Write list items so they have parallel structure
rule_summary: Write all list items using the same grammatical structure.
rule_detail: All items should start with the same word type (e.g. all verbs or all nouns) and use the same tense and sentence type. Mixing structures makes lists harder to scan and understand.
example_bad: - reading more emails\n- going to meetings\n- punctual.
example_good: - read more emails\n- go to meetings\n- be punctual.
pattern_hint: Check that the first token POS tag is consistent across all list items

source_heading: Write list items so they have parallel structure
rule_summary: Move repeated words from list items into the lead-in.
rule_detail: Words that appear in every list item are redundant in the items themselves. Moving them to the lead-in reduces repetition and improves readability.
pattern_hint: Detect identical leading tokens across all list items in a list

source_heading: Punctuate lead-ins and headings consistently
rule_summary: Always end phrase lead-ins with a colon.
rule_detail: Phrase lead-ins (incomplete sentences introducing a list) must always end with a colon (:). This is not optional — it is required by current government style.

source_heading: Punctuate lead-ins and headings consistently
rule_summary: End sentence lead-ins with either a colon or a full stop but use only one style throughout a document.
rule_detail: Sentence lead-ins may end with a colon or full stop. Whichever is chosen must be used consistently for all sentence lead-ins in the document. When in doubt a colon is preferred as the more common choice.

source_heading: Punctuate lead-ins and headings consistently
rule_summary: Do not add punctuation marks to headings that introduce lists.
rule_detail: Headings used in place of lead-ins must not end with a colon or any other punctuation mark. Punctuation on headings is not part of current government style.

source_heading: Use minimal punctuation for all lists
rule_summary: Do not use semicolons at the end of bullet or numbered list items.
rule_detail: Current government style requires minimal punctuation in lists. Semicolons at the end of list items are unnecessary and create visual clutter.
example_good: - read more emails

source_heading: Use minimal punctuation for all lists
rule_summary: Do not use commas at the end of bullet or numbered list items.
rule_detail: Current government style requires minimal punctuation in lists. Commas at the end of list items are unnecessary and should be removed.

source_heading: Use minimal punctuation for all lists
rule_summary: Do not use 'and' or 'or' after list items unless essential for legal clarity.
rule_detail: Minimal punctuation style omits conjunctions after list items. Only include 'and' or 'or' after the second-last item if the legal or logical meaning would otherwise be ambiguous. Note this in the lead-in.

source_heading: Use minimal punctuation for all lists
rule_summary: Do not write 'etc.' at the end of a list to indicate it is incomplete.
rule_detail: Using 'etc.' at the end of a list is not permitted under current government style. If a list is incomplete use an appropriate lead-in such as 'for example' or 'including' instead.
example_good: - islands\n- coral reefs

source_heading: Use minimal punctuation for all lists
rule_summary: Use 'for example' or 'including' in the lead-in to signal an incomplete list.
rule_detail: Lead-ins for incomplete lists should signal this with 'for example' or 'including' or 'includes'. This replaces the prohibited use of 'etc.' and is clearer for readers.
pattern_hint: Detect list preceded by lead-in lacking 'for example' or 'including' where list appears non-exhaustive

source_heading: Use full stops to complete sentences and fragment lists
rule_summary: Finish every item in a sentence list with a full stop.
rule_detail: Each item in a sentence list is a complete sentence and must end with a full stop, including the last item. Omitting full stops may cause screen readers to run list items into the following paragraph.

source_heading: Use full stops to complete sentences and fragment lists
rule_summary: Finish only the last item of a fragment list with a full stop.
rule_detail: Fragment list items are not complete sentences. Only the final item should end with a full stop; all preceding items should have no terminal punctuation. This signals the end of the list to screen readers.

source_heading: Use full stops to complete sentences and fragment lists
rule_summary: Do not end stand-alone list items with a full stop.
rule_detail: Stand-alone lists (introduced by a heading rather than a lead-in) do not use full stops on any item. Adding full stops to stand-alone list items is a formatting error.
example_good: - Answer phone enquiries

source_heading: Sentence lists
rule_summary: Start each sentence list item with a capital letter.
rule_detail: Sentence list items are complete sentences and must follow normal sentence structure, beginning with a capital letter. This is a basic grammatical requirement for sentence lists.

source_heading: Sentence lists
rule_summary: Avoid including multiple sentences in a single sentence list item.
rule_detail: Each item in a sentence list should contain only one sentence. Multiple sentences per item make the list harder to scan and dilute the list format's benefit for users.
pattern_hint: Detect list items containing more than one sentence boundary (full stop followed by capital letter within item)

source_heading: Sentence lists
rule_summary: Align run-over lines of sentence list items with the text not the bullet or number.
rule_detail: When a sentence list item wraps to a second line the continuation should align with the text character not the bullet or number character. This improves readability and visual consistency.

source_heading: Fragment lists
rule_summary: Start fragment list items with a lower-case letter unless the item begins with a proper noun.
rule_detail: Fragment list items are not complete sentences so they should not begin with a capital letter, unless the first word is a proper noun. This distinguishes fragments from sentence lists.
example_bad: - Islands and coral reefs\n- Abundant wildlife
example_good: - islands and coral reefs\n- abundant wildlife

source_heading: Fragment lists
rule_summary: Introduce fragment lists with a sentence or phrase lead-in followed by a colon.
rule_detail: Fragment lists must have a lead-in that ends with a colon. The lead-in frames the fragments so that each item grammatically completes the lead-in as a sentence.

source_heading: Fragment lists
rule_summary: Ensure each fragment list item grammatically completes the lead-in as a sentence.
rule_detail: Each fragment must make grammatical sense when read together with the lead-in. If an item cannot complete the lead-in the list structure or lead-in needs revision.

source_heading: Stand-alone lists
rule_summary: Introduce stand-alone lists with a heading not a lead-in sentence.
rule_detail: Stand-alone lists appear under a heading rather than a prose lead-in. Using a sentence lead-in instead of a heading is incorrect for this list type.

source_heading: Stand-alone lists
rule_summary: Do not end the heading of a stand-alone list with a colon.
rule_detail: The heading that introduces a stand-alone list must not end with a colon or other punctuation mark. Colons are reserved for phrase and sentence lead-ins not headings.
example_good: My weekly tasks

source_heading: Stand-alone lists
rule_summary: Start each stand-alone list item with a capital letter.
rule_detail: Stand-alone list items begin with a capital letter. This distinguishes them from fragment list items, which begin with lower case.

source_heading: Use consistent formatting for all lists
rule_summary: Do not mix different list types within a single list.
rule_detail: A single list must use only one list type throughout. Mixing sentence list items with fragment items or stand-alone items within the same list is a formatting error.

source_heading: Write numbered lists if the order is critical
rule_summary: Use a numbered list when the order of items is critical.
rule_detail: Numbered lists signal that sequence matters, such as in step-by-step instructions. If order is not critical use a bullet list instead.

source_heading: Write numbered lists if the order is critical
rule_summary: Avoid using in-line numbered lists.
rule_detail: In-line numbered lists (e.g. '1. item one 2. item two' within a paragraph) should not be used. Content that needs to be numbered should be formatted as a proper numbered list.

source_heading: Put unordered lists in a sequence that helps the user
rule_summary: Order unordered list items logically or alphabetically.
rule_detail: Unordered (bullet) lists should not be arranged arbitrarily. Items should follow a logical sequence or alphabetical order to help users find and understand information.

source_heading: Avoid using a multilevel list
rule_summary: Avoid using multilevel lists; use them only when necessary.
rule_detail: Multilevel lists add complexity and should be avoided. If a multilevel list is genuinely required it must have no more than 2 levels of nesting.

source_heading: Avoid using a multilevel list
rule_summary: Do not use more than 2 levels in a multilevel list.
rule_detail: If a multilevel list is used it must not exceed 2 levels of nesting. More than 2 levels creates complexity that makes content hard to follow.

source_heading: Avoid using a multilevel list
rule_summary: Use lowercase letters for the second level of a numbered multilevel list.
rule_detail: When a numbered multilevel list requires a second level the items at that level should use lowercase letters. This distinguishes second-level items from first-level numbered items.

source_heading: Avoid using a multilevel list
rule_summary: Use a dash for the second level of a bullet multilevel list.
rule_detail: When a bullet multilevel list requires a second level use a dash (–) for those items. This visually differentiates second-level items from first-level bullet items.

source_heading: Avoid using a multilevel list
rule_summary: Use the same style for all items at the same level of a multilevel list.
rule_detail: All items at the same level within a multilevel list must follow the same formatting style. Mixing styles at the same level is inconsistent and harder to read.
